title: Learn by Doing: Cache Mapping Functions
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on cache, each worked and then taught from nothing. This is the heaviest written topic on the paper.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, and no topic repeats like this one: splitting an address into fields has been set three times in a single paper, average memory access time in three separate years, and the locality definitions in three.

If you have time for one topic's Part B, make it this one.

lockin.big: "Offset bits come from the block size, line or set bits from how many lines or sets, and the tag is whatever is left of the address."
lockin.sub: Direct mapped: line equals block number modulo number of lines. Set associative: set equals block number modulo number of sets. Fully associative: no index at all, the tag is everything.

methodFrames.teach: A cache holds copies of blocks from main memory. The mapping function answers one question: given an address, where in the cache could that block be, and how do you know if it is the right one?
methodFrames.ask: Memory is 64 MB and blocks are 16 bytes. How many bits of the address pick a byte inside a block?

methodFrames.teach: Those are the offset or word bits, and they always come from the BLOCK SIZE alone. Nothing about the cache changes them.
methodFrames.ask: The cache holds 2K lines. How many bits pick the line, in a direct mapped cache?

methodFrames.teach: Those are the line bits, and they come from HOW MANY LINES the cache has. What remains of the address is the tag, and the tag is what is stored beside the data to prove which block is present.
methodFrames.ask: Memory is 64 MB, so how wide is the address, and what is the tag width here?

methodFrames.check: 26 bits of address, so the tag is 26 minus 11 minus 4, which is 11 bits.
methodFrames.teach: Always in that order: address width, offset, index, tag is the rest. Write the three widths as a labelled diagram of the address and the marks are unmissable.
methodFrames.ask: Now make it 4 way set associative with the same cache size. What changes?

methodFrames.check: The index counts SETS, not lines, and there are four times fewer sets, so one bit moves to the tag.
methodFrames.teach: Set associative: number of sets equals lines divided by associativity, and set equals block number modulo number of sets. Fully associative has no index at all: the tag is everything above the offset, and every line must be searched.
methodFrames.ask: Second family: average memory access time, with a hit rate of 80 per cent, cache 5 ns and memory 100 ns. Two organizations are asked for. What is the difference?

methodFrames.check: Simultaneous access starts both at once; hierarchical access tries the cache first and only then memory.
methodFrames.teach: Simultaneous: AMAT equals hit rate times cache time plus miss rate times memory time, so 0.8 times 5 plus 0.2 times 100, which is 24 ns. Hierarchical: a miss costs the cache time AND the memory time, so 0.8 times 5 plus 0.2 times 105, which is 25 ns. One number apart, and the examiner wants both.
methodFrames.ask: Last family, the free marks: locality of reference, temporal and spatial.

methodFrames.check: Programs reuse what they used recently, and use what is nearby.
methodFrames.teach: Write three labelled lines. Locality of reference: a program accesses a small part of its address space at any time. Temporal: an item used now is likely to be used again soon, which justifies keeping it. Spatial: items near it are likely next, which justifies fetching a whole block. Then one closing line: cache exists because both hold.

exam.problem: Given 32-bit address ; 16 words per block ; direct-mapped, 256 blocks
exam.answer:
Find the cache line each hex address maps to, in decimal
Formula offset = log2(words/block) ; index = log2(lines) ; the index field IS the line
offset = log2(16) = 4 bits    (one hex digit)
index  = log2(256) = 8 bits   (two hex digits)
So: drop the last hex digit (offset), read the next two (the line):

  CA2DFC1|2   ->  C1  =  193
  F24F25F|F   ->  5F  =  95
  24BBABC|D   ->  BC  =  188
  C1D9EEF|2   ->  EF  =  239
Lines: CA2DFC12 → 193, F24F25FF → 95, 24BBABCD → 188, C1D9EEF2 → 239.

exam.problem: Given main memory 1 GB ; cache 512 KB ; block 128 B ; 4-way ; h = 0.96, Tc = 2 ns, Tm = 80 ns
exam.answer:
Find blocks, sets, the address format, the AMAT
Formula blocks = cache/block ; sets = blocks/ways ; tag = addr − set − offset ; AMAT = Tc + (1−h)×Tm
Blocks = 512 KB / 128 B = 2¹⁹ / 2⁷ = 4096
Sets   = 4096 / 4 = 1024
Address = 1 GB = 2³⁰ -> 30 bits
  offset = log2(128) = 7
  set    = log2(1024) = 10
  tag    = 30 - 10 - 7 = 13
AMAT = Tc + (1-h)Tm = 2 + 0.04 x 80 = 2 + 3.2 = 5.2 ns
4096 blocks; 1024 sets; address tag 13 / set 10 / offset 7; AMAT 5.2 ns. (v) More ways cuts conflict misses but needs more tag comparators, so beyond a point it adds cost and delay for little gain.

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Given main memory 64 MB ; cache 128 KB ; block 64 B
Find lines ; direct fields ; 4-way fields ; the fully-associative trade-off
Formula lines = cache/block ; offset = log2(block) ; tag = addr − index(or set) − offset
Lines = 128 KB / 64 B = 2¹⁷ / 2⁶ = 2¹¹ = 2048
Address = 64 MB = 2²⁶ -> 26 bits ; offset = log2(64) = 6

Direct: index = log2(2048) = 11 ; tag = 26 - 11 - 6 = 9
4-way : sets = 2048/4 = 512 ; set = log2(512) = 9 ; tag = 26 - 9 - 6 = 11
2048 lines. Direct: index 11, tag 9, offset 6. 4-way: set 9, tag 11, offset 6. (iv) Fully associative lets any block go in any line, so no conflict misses, but every line's tag must be searched, which is slow and costly.

exam.problem: i) Locality of reference is defined as the tendency of a program to keep accessing the same small set of memory locations over a short period, a consequence of loops and subroutines; it is why a small fast cache can satisfy most accesses.
exam.answer: ii) Temporal (time) locality is defined as: if a memory location is accessed, it is very likely to be accessed again soon (the same instruction or variable reused). Its partner, spatial (space) locality, is defined as: if a location is accessed, the nearby addresses are very likely to be accessed next (as when stepping through an array).

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given a cache hit rate of 80%, a cache access time of 5 ns and a main memory access time of 100 ns. Nothing else, so the miss rate 20% is yours to derive.
Asked determine the average access time twice, once under each organisation, and then draw both. Three separate deliverables under one part.
Marks 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. The 3 sits on the diagrams, which is the largest single share, so a part answered with numbers only throws away nearly half of it.
Taught in Module Three Unit 3, Cache Memory Design.
Trap using one formula for both. Simultaneous access starts cache and main memory together, so the cache time is not paid twice; hierarchical pays the cache time on every access and the memory time again on a miss. The answers differ by 1 ns, and a copied formula scores zero on one of the two.
Given h = 0.80 · Tc = 5 ns · Tm = 100 ns
Find AMAT under both organisations
Formula simultaneous = h×Tc + (1−h)×Tm · hierarchical = Tc + (1−h)×Tm
Simultaneous = 0.8(5) + 0.2(100) = 4 + 20 = 24 ns. Hierarchical = 5 + 0.2(100) = 5 + 20 = 25 ns. Diagrams: simultaneous shows the CPU addressing cache and main memory in parallel; hierarchical shows the CPU reaching main memory only through the cache. Hierarchical is 1 ns slower here because the cache time is paid on every access, hit or miss.

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given a 24-bit address, 16 words per block, a direct-mapped cache of 256 blocks, and four addresses written in hexadecimal.
Asked in which block (line) each address lands. One number per address, four numbers in all.
Marks 6 for four addresses, so roughly 1½ each with the remainder for showing the field split once. Do the split once, then apply it four times.
Taught in Module Three Unit 3, Cache Memory Design.
Trap counting bits when you could count hex digits. 4 offset bits are exactly one hex digit and 8 index bits are exactly two, so the line is the two digits before the last. Also give the answer in decimal and say so, since the paper leaves the base of the answer open.
Given address = 24 bits · block = 16 words · cache = 256 blocks · mapping = direct
Find the cache block (line) for each address
Formula offset = log216 = 4 bits · index = log2256 = 8 bits · tag = 24 − 8 − 4 = 12 bits · the index field is the line number
reading it off the hex 4 offset bits are exactly one hex digit, and 8 index bits are exactly two. So in a 6-digit address, drop the last digit and the next two digits are the line.
AddressOffset (last digit)Line (next two digits)Line in decimal
1A2BC00BC188
FFFF000F0240
12345664569
C109D559D157
Blocks: 1A2BC0 → 188, FFFF00 → 240, 123456 → 69, C109D5 → 157. Address format: tag 12, line 8, offset 4.

scenario.text: a. i) Describe how cache memory improves the performance of a computer system. 2mks ii) Using the specifications below, design a cache system for each of Direct, Fully Associative and 2-way Set Associative Mapping. iii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of each method. 8mks specifications: - Cache size: 1 KB = 1024 bytes - Block size: 16 bytes - Main memory size: 64 KB = 65,536 bytes - Address size: 16 bits

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given cache 1 KB, block 16 bytes, main memory 64 KB, address 16 bits, and three mapping schemes to apply them to.
Asked three verbs. Describe how cache improves performance, design the cache under each of three mappings, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of each. Nine separate statements in the last part alone.
Marks 2 + 8 = 10, half of Question Two. The design and the trade offs share 8, so budget roughly 5 for the three address formats and 3 for the six verdicts.
Taught in Module Three Unit 3, Cache Memory Design.
Trap recomputing the line count for each mapping. It is 1 KB / 16 B = 64 lines under all three; only the way those lines are addressed changes. The other trap is answering "design" with prose: the mark is for a tag, index and offset split in bits.
Given cache = 1 KB · block = 16 bytes · main memory = 64 KB · address = 16 bits
Find the address format under each of the three mappings, plus one advantage and one disadvantage each
Formula lines = cache / block · offset = log2(block) · sets = lines / k · tag = address − index (or set) − offset · tag directory = lines × tag bits
what each symbol means lines = 1 KB / 16 B = 64, the same under all three mappings · offset = log216 = 4 bits · k = the ways per set, 2 for the 2-way case · 64 KB = 216, which is why the address is 16 bits
MappingTagIndex / setOffsetTag directory
Direct66 (index, 64 lines)464 × 6 = 384 bits = 48 bytes
Fully associative12none464 × 12 = 768 bits = 96 bytes
2-way set assoc.75 (set, 32 sets)464 × 7 = 448 bits = 56 bytes
Direct: simplest and fastest lookup (one line to check, one comparator), but two blocks mapping to the same line evict each other, causing conflict misses. Fully associative: no conflict misses, any block may sit anywhere, but every line's tag must be compared at once, which is expensive and slow, and the tag directory doubles to 96 bytes. 2-way: the compromise, most conflict misses removed for only two comparators and a modest tag growth to 56 bytes.

scenario.text: b. i) Explain the following terms: 4½mks 1. Locality of reference 2. Temporal locality 3. Special Locality ii) What happens when there is a Cache Miss? 1½ mks

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given nothing numeric. This is a definitions part, four terms in all if you count the cache miss.
Asked explain, not merely name, three terms, then say what happens on a cache miss. The second verb wants a sequence of events, not a definition.
Marks 4½ + 1½ = 6, so 1½ per term in (i). That is two or three sentences each, with an example, not one line.
Taught in Module Three Unit 1, Computer Memory Overview.
Trap correcting the paper. Answer the third term as spatial locality, but keep the examiner's numbering and do not waste a line pointing out the spelling. The other trap is defining temporal and spatial without first defining locality of reference, which is the term the other two are special cases of.
(i) Locality of reference is the tendency of a program to access a small, predictable set of memory locations during any short period. Temporal: a location used now is likely to be used again soon, so cache keeps recently used items. Spatial: locations near one just used are likely to be used soon, so cache fetches a whole block of neighbours at once. (ii) On a miss the word is not in cache, so the address goes onto the system bus, main memory returns the whole block containing it, that block is loaded into a cache line (evicting one if necessary), and the required word is delivered to the CPU at the same time.

questions.heading: 2023/2024, Q1(d)

scenario.text: d. If an 8-way set association cache is made up of 32 bits words, 4 words per line and 4096 sets. i) Size of each line of the cache 1mk ii) Size of each set of the cache 1mk iii) Size of the cache itself 1mk

questions.asked: Set once, in 2023/2024. It is still the examiner's own question, and the method behind it is on the syllabus.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given 8 ways to a set, a 32-bit word, 4 words to a line, and 4096 sets.

Asked three sizes, each written as a noun phrase, "Size of each line of the cache". A number with a unit is the whole of the answer.

Marks 1mk each. There is no working mark on offer, so give the number and one line showing where it came from.

Taught in this unit, Module Three Unit 3.

Trap 32 bits is 4 bytes. Answering in bits where the natural unit is bytes, or multiplying by 32 where you meant 4, is where this one is lost. Build up in order: line, then set, then cache.

exam.problem: Answer 2023/2024 Q1(d) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given k = 8 (8-way) · word = 32 bits = 4 bytes · 4 words per line · 4096 sets
Find the size of a line, of a set, and of the whole cache
Formula line = words per line × word size · set = k × line size · cache = sets × set size
what each symbol means k = 8, the lines per set · a 32-bit word is 4 bytes, and mixing the two units is the classic slip here · build it up in order, line then set then cache, and the arithmetic stays trivial
  1. Line size = 4 words × 32 bits = 4 × 4 bytes = 16 bytes.
  2. Set size = 8 lines × 16 bytes = 128 bytes.
  3. Cache size = 4096 sets × 128 bytes = 524 288 bytes = 512 KB.
Line 16 bytes, set 128 bytes, cache 512 KB.

questions.heading: 2023/2024, Q3(a)

scenario.text: a. Determine the average memory access time for a machine with a cache hit rate of 80% and cache access time of 5 ns and main memory access time of 100 ns when. i. Simultaneous access memory organization is used. 2½mks ii. Hierarchical access memory organization is used. 2½mks iii.Draw the diagrams representing the two scenarios 3mks

questions.asked: This question repeats. The same question, average memory access time, simultaneous against hierarchical, was also set in 2024/2025 Q1(b). Wording and numbers move; the method does not.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given a hit rate of 80%, a cache access time of 5 ns, and a main memory access time of 100 ns.

Asked the average access time under two named organisations, then the diagrams. The two names, "Simultaneous" and "Hierarchical", are the whole question: they choose which of the two formulas applies.

Marks 2 + 2 + 3 in 24/25, and 2½ + 2½ + 3 in 23/24. Either way the diagrams are worth more than either calculation, so draw them.

Taught in this unit, Module Three Unit 3.

Trap the two formulas differ in one place only: whether the cache time is weighted by the hit rate or paid on every access. Simultaneous starts both lookups at once; hierarchical searches the cache first. Give both numbers and label which is which.

exam.problem: Answer 2023/2024 Q3(a) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given h = 0.80 · Tc = 5 ns · Tm = 100 ns · both organisations required
Find the AMAT under (i) simultaneous and (ii) hierarchical organisation
Formula simultaneous = h×Tc + (1−h)×Tm · hierarchical = Tc + (1−h)×Tm
what each symbol means h = hit ratio · Tc, Tm = cache and main-memory access times · the only difference between the two formulas is whether the cache time is weighted by h (simultaneous, both started at once) or paid in full every time (hierarchical, cache searched first)
  1. Simultaneous: AMAT = h×Tc + (1−h)×Tm = 0.8×5 + 0.2×100 = 4 + 20 = 24 ns.
  2. Hierarchical: AMAT = Tc + (1−h)×Tm = 5 + 0.2×100 = 5 + 20 = 25 ns.
Simultaneous 24 ns, hierarchical 25 ns. Hierarchical pays the cache time on every access (even misses), so it is slightly slower here.

Now redo it: the difference is only whether the cache time is always paid (hierarchical) or only on hits (simultaneous). Learn both formulas.

questions.heading: 2023/2024, Q3(c)

scenario.text: c. Explain the following 4½mks i) Locality of reference ii) Temporal locality iii) Spacial Locality

questions.asked: This question repeats. The same question, locality of reference, temporal and spatial, was also set in 2025/2026 Q5(c), 2024/2025 Q2(b). Wording and numbers move; the method does not.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given nothing but the terms. This is a definition question, not a calculation.

Asked "Explain", which is neither "define" nor "list". An explanation names the idea, says why it holds, and says what the machine does about it.

Marks 3mks for two terms in 25/26 and 4½mks for three in the two older papers, so about 1½ marks a term. That is a sentence of definition plus a sentence of consequence, each.

Taught in this unit, the Teach box directly above.

Trap the misspelling. Do not lose time in the hall wondering whether "Special Locality" or "Spacial Locality" is a fourth concept you have never met. It is spatial locality both times.

exam.problem: Answer 2023/2024 Q3(c) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer: Locality of reference is the tendency of a program to access a small, predictable set of memory locations during any short period. Temporal locality: a location accessed now is likely to be accessed again soon (so cache keeps recently used items). Spatial locality: locations near one just accessed are likely to be accessed soon (so cache fetches a whole block of neighbouring words at once).
